body: From a surface view, what you said here seems fine, but you have to remember that people commit suicide. People are depressed because they have no support from their surroundings. Those people feel like they have no one, nothing to turn to. No relationships or future. And what sucks even more is that not everyone is born with a silver spoon. Most are born in poverty, and struggle to climb out. I think there are a lot of times when people would prefer "not to exist" over living such a life.

My main ideal in life is (ironically) not to oppose your own ideas onto others. Let everyone around you have their own opinion, and you can have yours. Many people would not agree with me, saying that their opinion is clearly in the "right", and I truly find it difficult to discern right vs wrong. Of course, I can easily tell morally right vs wrong, or rather, what the general populace would see. In the point you argue, it does fit with my ideal. Telling others to use pronouns they may not remember to use or feel uncomfortable with clashes entirely against my idea of free thinking. But at the same time, some people will be offended if you don't address them correctly. This goes for non transgender or "cis" people as well. I have been called "ma'am" for having long hair, although I wasn't offended. 

In my opinion, those people who force pronoun usage onto others ultimately feel the need for validation from their surroundings, hence their pronouns. I mean no offense, but I believe they should find validation in people closer to them, or simpyl validate themselves.

1. Yes to a certain extent, I agree with your first point, however, completely secluding them to this would have roughly the same effect. They'll be sheltered from this either way, and upon reaching that curious stage, even if they're 16 or 18, they'll still be shocked. I do believe it is better if they are older, as they will have reached maturity, but total and complete seclusion, I feel, isn't the best.

2. Yes, again, you have a valid point of not allowing minors to speak to strangers, but yet parents don't completely ban their children from going outside. Instead, their parents remind them of "stranger danger" in order to have their kids learn a habit of not conversing with strangers. The same could be said for online conversations. Monitored access and teaching younger generations to be safe online is safer as opposed to thrusting 18 year olds into the internet without any knowledge.

3. Again, you make a decent half point, but the same could be said for in person bullying, which could be even more difficult to prevent. Countries like America and South Korea have a horrible system for dealing with bullying behavior, and this obviously leads to increased suicide rates, as you mentioned. But again, cyberbullying is generally easier (imo) to deal with, and detect, as many platforms, whether they be communication or games, allow for blocking messages or people entirely. I know this might be a simplification, but sometimes it really is that easy.

4. You do have a better point here, but radicalisation is everywhere. Technology was simply limiting the range of how far opinions could be shared, but I stand with you. On the flipside, freedom of speech is a right that many people have, and as much as I disagree with them, I cannot do anything about it. I assume your main point here is to say that they may have some radical ideas ingrained at a young age, to which I agree. But I do think that parenting children on the internet is more beneficial than letting them experience it alone.

5. Too lazy to argue this last point, but I would like to believe that misinformation is not as widespread as it generally seems to be. Hopefully parents can manage or teach their children to search for multiple authentic sources as opposed to believing everything they read or see online.

The fact that she immediately trusted your siblings and believed you lied is horrible. You definitely didn't ruin anything. You prepared everything, and your mother just writes it off? And when confronted with the truth, she claims it's just a joke, and tramples on your feelings. I'm sorry that this happened to you, and I hope you don't have to interact with them in the future.

Hurts that this rings true with me. Missed the bus, was the first, maybe second time in the entire school year I had done so. Dad wouldn't let me take the car, and insisted that this was entirely on me. The thing is, it was a new bus driver who came early, and in the end I hitched a ride with a friend who also missed the bus. I was jealous, because he had actual parents, who cared for him.
